title: LISTEN: How Chris Carter Got a Second Shot at ‘The X-Files: I Want to Believe’ Film
description: On today’s episode of “Daily Variety” podcast, “The X-Files” creator Chris Carter explains to Variety’s Michael Schneider how he got the chance to d
body:
On today’s episode of “Daily Variety” podcast, “The X-Files” creator Chris Carter explains to Variety’s Michael Schneider how he got the chance to do a director’s cut of his 2008 “The X-Files: I Want to Believe” feature film. The new cut dubbed “The X-Files: I Wanted to Believe: Vrach Frankenshteyn” debuted Aug. 14 on Hulu and Disney+ outside the U.S.

	Carter points out that his preferred cut is actually shorter than the original release, which ran 144 minutes, per IMDB.
	

	“I always felt like people didn’t see the movie I intended to make,” Carter says, noting that 20th Century Studios executive Steve Asbell helped get the director’s cut project off the ground. “I asked him, ‘Have you ever thought about doing a director’s cut?’ And it was really just offhand. And he said, ‘Why? Would you like to do one?’ I said, ‘I’d love to do one.’ I can tell you, though, the reason for doing the director’s cut for me is not to put all the stuff that was taken out, but to put the right stuff in that was taken out.” 


	Carter discloses that for the original release in 2008, he was under a lot of pressure to ensure that the film would secure at PG-13 rating. 

	“When we showed them our first cut, the studio freaked out. They said, ‘This is torture porn. And you can’t do this for a PG-13 movie.’ So we cut it back and we satisfied them. And then we gave it to the motion picture folks, and they said, this isn’t a PG-13 movie. And we cut it back even further,” Carter says. “So the movie you’re seeing is, by and large, the movie that my partner in crime, [writer-producer] Frank Spotnitz, and I set out to make. And we always set out to make a very scary movie on a very limited budget, which is kind of the way we made ‘The X Files‘ TV series.”
	

	Listen to Daily Variety on iHeartPodcasts, Apple Podcasts, Variety’s YouTube Podcast channel, Amazon Music, Spotify and other podcast platforms.

schema.headline: LISTEN: How Chris Carter Got a Second Shot at ‘The X-Files: I Want to Believe’ Film

title: ‘Friday the 13th’ Prequel Series ‘Crystal Lake’ Is ‘Gory’ and ‘Gross’ With ‘Blood Everywhere,’ Says Star Linda Cardellini
description:
“Crystal Lake” star Linda Cardellini is teasing the upcoming “Friday the 13th” prequel television series.

	Cardellini stars in the Peacock series a
body:
“Crystal Lake” star Linda Cardellini is teasing the upcoming “Friday the 13th” prequel television series.

	Cardellini stars in the Peacock series as the franchise antagonist Pamela Voorhees. The show, premiering Oct. 15 on the streamer, follows Voorhees’ life prior to the events of the first “Friday the 13th” film. It also stars William Catlett as Levon Brooks, though exact character details remain under wraps. 


	“I remember one of my most fun moviegoing experiences was I saw ‘Freddy vs. Jason’ on the Universal City Walk, which is a giant movie theater, at the height of its popularity, and people were screaming at the screen and throwing things,” she told me Sunday at the HBO Max Emmy Nominee Celebration event in Hollywood.
	

	Does she predict the same for the new TV show? “This is a longer format so there’s a lot more you get to do in eight episodes,” Cardellini said. “It’s not necessarily like 90 minutes of pure horror. There’s a lot of story there. So maybe once in a while you’ll throw some things and scream.”

	And possibly cover your eyes.

	“It does get gory, yes, so much so that I wish sometimes they weren’t as practical as they were,” Cardellini said. “There’s a couple of gory moments on set that were very practical that were pretty gross. Blood everywhere at one point.”

Linda Cardellini teases the upcoming “Friday the 13th” prequel series, "Crystal Lake": “This is a longer format so there’s a lot more you get to do in eight episodes,” Cardellini said. “It’s not necessarily like 90 minutes of pure horror. There’s a lot of story there. So maybe… pic.twitter.com/NCB60HsEYq— Variety (@Variety) August 17, 2026


	Cardellini said most horror scripts she’s given are for characters who are running away from the killer. “Everything that I’ve ever read that was handed to me that was in that space was for the person who was being chased, not the person who was chasing everyone,” she said. “It was really fun this time to be on the other side of the knife.”
	

	Pamela first appeared in the original “Friday the 13th” movie in 1980 as Jason’s mother. She exacts revenge on people who she believed were responsible for Jason’s drowning in 1957 at Camp Crystal Lake.

	Cardellini attended the HBO Max Emmy event to celebrate her nomination for her work in “DTF St. Louis.”

schema.headline: ‘Friday the 13th’ Prequel Series ‘Crystal Lake’ Is ‘Gory’ and ‘Gross’ With ‘Blood Everywhere,’ Says Star Linda Cardellini

title: ‘Furious’ Star Steve Way on the Beauty of ‘Disabled Love’ and the Difficulty of Navigating Hollywood Without a Team: ‘I Want an Agency to Whore Me Out’
description: It’s uncommon to meet an actor bold enough to call Ari Emanuel, the executive chairman of WME Group and one of the most powerful people in Hollywood
body:
It’s uncommon to meet an actor bold enough to call Ari Emanuel, the executive chairman of WME Group and one of the most powerful people in Hollywood, a “prick” on the record.

	But it’s also uncommon to interview an actor as unfiltered as Steve Way.

	“I want an agency to whore me out,” he says. “Let’s make a ton of money together. Let’s change the world.” I joke that I’ll pass along his exact words to all the big companies. “Just get Ari on the phone,” he retorts. “Ari loves me. Except he won’t hire me.” That’s when Way mutters the p-word — under his breath for plausible deniability, but certainly still with the intention of being heard, smirking at the sound of my laughter. This is one of the last things he says to me before we wrap up our interview. A light blue Labubu that he’s clipped to his motorized wheelchair gives a wink as he rolls away.
	

	It’s impossible to fault Way, 35, for his ire. That’s partially because it’s well delivered — he’s got 15 years of stand-up comedy under his belt — but mostly because he works in an industry that seems determined to shut out people like him. Best known for his recurring role in Ramy Youssef’s self-titled dramedy series, and now giving an impeccable supporting performance in Hulu’s “Furious,” Way has no agent or manager. “And we know why,” he says, referring to his chair, his ventilator and the muscular dystrophy diagnosis he received at age 4.


	“I don’t have representation. And it’s frustrating, because I used to,” Way says. With his first agent, he got “nothing. Just nothing.” He signed with someone new, who later jumped to another agency and didn’t bring Way with him.
	



	

					Left to right: Ramy Youssef, Steve Way and Bella Hadid in “Ramy” Season 3.
									Courtesy of Hulu
	



	Way spent years wondering whether he’d be able to book a project without the support of Youssef, a close friend since childhood. Then, with “Furious,” he received something actors spend their whole careers dreaming of: a role written expressly for him.

	“Furious” is helmed by Elizabeth Meriwether, the writer-producer famed for creating “New Girl” and “The Dropout,” whom Way first met in 2025 when they appeared together on a WGA panel about on-screen depictions of caregiving. “I did the panel really high,” Way admits. He’d been on a stand-up tour as Youssef’s opener, and needed to relax after all the travel. “We’re going down the line talking about what we’re working on. Full resumes. And it got to me, and I was like, ‘I’m unemployed. If anyone wants to put me in their stuff, [I’ll join] gladly,’” Way recalls. Meriwether took his stoned comments to heart. “Two months later, I got an email from her people saying she wrote a part for me. That was it.”

	Way stars in the series as the love interest of the serial killer played by Lola Petticrew. To everyone else, Catherine is a sociopath. But to Alden, she’s simply a kindhearted in-home health aide who perhaps has a few secrets. As she feeds and bathes him with a gentle touch and a warm gaze, he returns the favor by giving her the benefit of the doubt about her shady comings and goings. Wanting to make the most of the time he has left after learning from doctors that his health has seriously worsened, Alden later proposes to Catherine with his late mother’s engagement ring, then begins abetting her crimes.

	There’s a profound sadness to the role, but “Furious” still makes plenty of room for the humor Way is known for. He applauds Meriwether for writing a disabled character who confronts his mortality but still has an identity beyond that, including a sense of humor. “When I read my first line — ‘You little slut!’ — I thought, ‘How does Liz know I would say that?” he says, smiling. “Right away, I knew that she would do the character justice.”

	When Danny (Scoot McNairy), a cop, suggests that Catherine is using him, Alden is resolute. “I don’t fucking care,” he says. “You think love is only when people do everything that you want them to do. That’s fucked up.”
	

	Way intimately understands that sentiment. “Everything is transactional. And as a disabled person, it’s very empowering to understand that. Caregiving is a two-way street. It has to be in order to work.” And the concept, in his eyes, isn’t exclusive to the relationship between disabled people and their aides. “Society has told a lot of lies about disabled people, mostly that we’re a burden. It’s not true. And to understand that is to accept that everyone, at some point in their life, receives care.”

	“When you take the subway, you don’t do that alone. Someone’s driving,” Way continues. “When you get DoorDash, that’s a level of care. So when Alden says that to Scoot’s character, in a way, he’s trying to radicalize him. Like, ‘You don’t get it, man.’” Smiling, he offers a phrase borrowed from his friend Danny Kurtzman, a fellow actor-producer with muscular dystrophy. “’Disabled love is the best love.’ Because of how intimate it is. How close you have to be,” he says.



	

					Lola Petticrew and Steve Way in “Furious.”
									Courtesy of Disney
	



	In Way’s opinion, “Alden and Catherine have the best relationship in the show: They had to get everything [uncomfortable] out of the way first and set up boundaries to make sure they could handle it. Like, ‘What’s your history with this person who’s keeping you alive? What do I do for them?’ It’s delicate, but there have to be boundaries, because it’s easy for any caregiver to get burnt out. That was really fun to figure out.”

	“Furious” was everything Way would have hoped for in terms of disability accommodations, thanks to the help of an on-set accessibility coordinator. “She made sure I was OK and advocated for me when I was really in the zone. Not once did I ever feel unsafe or not taken care of. It allowed me to just focus on the character. I wanted to feel the love and trust, to find our routines. Like, how would she would shower me? But also something as delicate as: How do we sit across from each other? How do we face each other lying down in a bed?”

	There were still moments when Way found himself pushing against his limits, physically. “There were some scenes that were uncomfortable — lying down for any extended period,” he says. But the discomfort was worth it to him. “I was locked in. Nothing else mattered; I just turned it off. The only thing that matters is the art that we’re operating here. That was my temporary. Yeah, the art. That’s it. The right thing for art, you know. That’s something that I realized no one can take away from me.
	

	Before “Furious,” Way wasn’t sure if his three-season run on “Ramy” had been enough to prove his talents to the industry. “I was scared people wouldn’t take me seriously. One time could be a fluke,” he says. “But twice? I’m pretty good at this.”



	

									Courtesy of Disney
	



	There’s still a long road ahead. Twice, Way has worked with a studio to develop a series he would create and star in himself, but both Apple TV and NBCUniversal ultimately passed. “It’s about the inner workings of a facility for disabled people,” he says. “We want to have a full disabled cast and show what it’s like to live in one building with not enough caregivers, with an administration who has no idea what they’re doing, in a country that doesn’t treat us the best. I think a lot of people will relate to it, and they’ll see the absurdity in our day-to-day.” 

	Slyly, he adds, “Shoutout Netflix!” — the streamer he hopes will be his next suitor.

	He’s gone through something similar with his stand-up comedy. He dreams of headlining his own tour. “It’s so hard to find accessible venues, but they’re out there. I gotta do my hour first, though,” he says. He’s already prepared — and taped — a full set he feels ready to show the world. He just hasn’t found a platform willing to help him turn it into a special. “Shoutout HBO!” he says.

	It’s par for the course at this point. “I’m numb to the noes,” Way says. “Because the noes have never stopped. And that’s OK. That’s just life; it’s no one’s fault. But it’s tough, because I have these big opportunities, and I don’t trust them.” With “Furious,” he tells me, he didn’t fully believe he’d get to be on TV again until his first day on set. “So when I hear that someone is interested in my show, I’ll take a meeting, but I don’t expect anything.”

	Still, he’s built more than he ever imagined for himself when he was younger. “I didn’t think I could have a career of any kind, because everyone told me I wouldn’t live long,” he says. “I almost died when I was 14, and I wasn’t supposed to live past 18. Then, when I was 25, my doctors told me I’m good. I was like, ‘Fuck! What now?’ I wasn’t good at anything besides telling jokes.” 

	So he keeps telling them. “The only thing that’s gonna stop me is my heart,” he says.
	

	And he’s also starting to enjoy the effects of the opportunity Meriwether gave him in “Furious.” For the first time, Way has a publicist, which he says has been “wonderful.”

	“It’s nice to respond to emails for once instead of initiating them, which is what I do every day,” Way says. Without a team behind him, the burden of seeking out the few roles available to disabled actors falls on him alone. “It’s tiring,” he says. “Espresso helps. Vodka helps. But I can’t run on that stuff forever.”

schema.headline: ‘Furious’ Star Steve Way on the Beauty of ‘Disabled Love’ and the Difficulty of Navigating Hollywood Without a Team: ‘I Want an Agency to Whore Me Out’

title: Netflix’s ‘A Different World’ Sequel Series Unveils Trailer, New Images
description:
School is back in session at Hillman College. Netflix’s new “A Different World” series released the official trailer and new images.

	The series is
body:
School is back in session at Hillman College. Netflix’s new “A Different World” series released the official trailer and new images.

	The series is a followup to the NBC sitcom of the same title, which ran from 1987 to 1993 and was itself a spin-off of “The Cosby Show.” It stars Jasmine Guy and Kadeem Hardison, reprising their roles as Whitley Gilbert and Dwayne Wayne, with Maleah Joi Moon as their youngest child Deborah, now starting her freshman year of college.
	

	The trailer welcomes a new generation to Hillman College, a fictional HBCU, and introduces the people that will become Deborah’s people. As Deborah attempts to make her own path at Hillman, her very-involved parents have their experiences to share about their alma mater. 


	The cast also features Alijah Kai, Cornell Young IV, Kennedi Reece, Jordan Aaron Hall and Chibuikem Uche. Along with Hardison and Guy, other original cast members including Darryl M. Bell, Debbie Allen, Cree Summer, Jenifer Lewis and Jada Pinkett Smith return to Hillman.

	“A Different World” is created by showrunner, writer and executive producer Felicia Pride. Allen, who was a director and producer on the original run, returns to executive and produce the sequel’s premiere. Tom Werner, Reggie Rock Bythewood, Gina Prince-Bythewood and Mandy Summers are executive producers.

	The original “A Different World” series aired for six seasons. Whitley and Dwayne were at the center of the show following the departure of Lisa Bonet as Denise Huxtable after the first season.

	Watch the full trailer below.

schema.headline: Netflix’s ‘A Different World’ Sequel Series Unveils Trailer, New Images

title: California A.G. Rejects $1.88 Billion Paramount Bond, Says Company Wants a ‘Do-Over’ on Merger Delay
description: The California attorney general’s office fired back against Paramount’s request for a $1.88 billion bond on Monday, saying the company is seeking a
body:
The California attorney general’s office fired back against Paramount’s request for a $1.88 billion bond on Monday, saying the company is seeking a “do-over” on its agreement to delay the Warner Bros. merger until an antitrust trial next March.

	In a statement, the A.G.’s office argued that Paramount is a “sophisticated” company that knew it would face regulatory review when it agreed to pay Warner Bros. shareholders a $7 million-per-day ticking fee, and that California should not be made to bear the burden of that decision.
	

	“Bottom line: Paramount went into this process with eyes wide open,” the office said. “They are lying in a bed of their own making, and once again, trying to blackmail us to get us to back down.”


	California Attorney General Rob Bonta is leading a 12-state coalition to block the merger on the grounds that it will reduce competition in the theatrical and basic cable markets. Last month, Paramount agreed to hold off on closing the deal until after the case is resolved at trial, or until next June, whichever comes first.

	But Paramount was hoping for an earlier trial date — ideally in November. In a motion filed on Monday, the company argued that it will be forced to pay $1.7 billion in ticking fees to Warner Bros. shareholders if the case drags out until June 1, plus another $190 million in financing costs.

	Paramount argues that the states and the Writers Guild of America — which has filed its own antitrust suit — should be required to post a bond to cover its losses arising from the delay in the event that the deal is ultimately approved.
	

	Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin initially granted a 14-day restraining order to block the merger in July. In that order, she waived the requirement to post a bond, saying the states had shown they were acting in pursuit of “important public interests.”

	The states, the WGA and Paramount later entered a stipulation to delay the merger — the functional equivalent of a preliminary injunction — which did not include any bond requirement. Now that Martinez-Olguin has set the trial for March 2, Paramount is seeking to amend the agreement to include the $1.88 billion bond. Failing that, Paramount wants to dissolve the deal and allow the merger to close.

	“Paramount and Warner Bros. are two sophisticated companies who willfully decided to include a costly ticking fee as a provision in their merger contract. They knew this merger would undergo regulatory review; they knew it was not a done deal; and they chose to include it anyway,” the A.G.’s office said Monday. “What’s more, Paramount itself stipulated to the timing it is now protesting — they agreed to the dates and did not request a bond as a condition of agreeing not to close until after the trial, and potentially as late as June 2027.  Now, they’re trying to get a do-over.”

	In a statement on Monday, Paramount argued that the 12 states are defying a global consensus that the deal presents no issues of competitive harm and should be approved.

	“We remain confident that plaintiffs’ case is without merit and will defend our pro-competitive transaction in court,” the company said.

schema.headline: California A.G. Rejects $1.88 Billion Paramount Bond, Says Company Wants a ‘Do-Over’ on Merger Delay

title: Donald Trump Attacks CNN’s Kristen Holmes for Asking if He Spoke to North Korean Dictator: ‘You’re a Loud, Boisterous Person. Be Quiet!’
description: President Donald Trump grew angry at CNN‘s Kristen Holmes during a press briefing at the White House Monday, after she asked whether he had spoken w
body:
President Donald Trump grew angry at CNN‘s Kristen Holmes during a press briefing at the White House Monday, after she asked whether he had spoken with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un.

	“Quiet,” Trump told Holmes, CNN’s senior White House correspondent, after she queried the president about if Jong-un had asked Trump to curtail U.S. military exercises with South Korea. “You’re a loud, boisterous person. You’re faking news!”
	

	In a social media post Sunday, Trump had said that “Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea” and that he would instruct Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!”


	Holmes tried to follow up on her question to the president, saying, “I was trying to find out if you had been talking to Kim Jong-un, if he had asked you to scale back on those military exercises.” Trump, talking over her, said: “Be quiet! Be quiet! Be quiet! You’re a fake reporter and you report fake news.”

	Meanwhile, the White House lashed out at Holmes because during the same event, she asked Trump for his response to a remark by Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff about one of Trump’s aides. Earlier in the day at a campaign rally, Ossoff said that Trump “doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar,” referring to Natalie Harp, the president’s executive assistant. Harp was among the small group of Trump officials who (along with the president) were secretly escorted off the Qatar-donated Air Force One to a smaller military aircraft in Turkey because of a threat from Iran.
	

	Following the exchange in the Oval Office, the White House’s Rapid Response 47 account on X wrote, “.@KristenhCNN is a disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession. @POTUS hosts a hero lifeguard in the Oval Office and she uses it as an opportunity to take a cheap shot about one of President Trump’s staffers. These scumbags are the lowest of the low.” The press event Monday at the White House was meant to honor teenage lifeguard Ryder Williams, who rescued a 10-year-old boy at a beach in Santa Cruz, California, last month.

	The White House comms team followed that up with this comment: “.@KristenhCNN: Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.”

	In a statement responding to the White House attacks, CNN said, “Kristen Holmes is one of the most respected and accomplished journalists covering the White House. This afternoon, she did her job and asked the President of the United States a tough, relevant, and newsworthy question on behalf of the American people. Public officials are free to challenge reporting they disagree with, but personal attacks on journalists for asking questions are beneath the office and inconsistent with the principles of a free press. We stand firmly behind Kristen and reject these attacks in the strongest possible terms.”

schema.headline: Donald Trump Attacks CNN’s Kristen Holmes for Asking if He Spoke to North Korean Dictator: ‘You’re a Loud, Boisterous Person. Be Quiet!’

title: Ariel Levy, a New Yorker Staff Writer, Joins ’60 Minutes’ as Contributor
description: Ariel Levy, a staff writer at The New Yorker magazine who has analyzed sexuality in culture and profiled a number of political and cultural newsmake
body:
Ariel Levy, a staff writer at The New Yorker magazine who has analyzed sexuality in culture and profiled a number of political and cultural newsmakers, will join “60 Minutes” as a contributor, the latest journalist to join the show’s ranks as it is being remade by Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News.

	“Ariel is an astonishingly original writer and reporter, fearlessly going to far-flung places and exploring sensitive topics that have driven consequential debates,” said Nick Bilton, recently installed as executive producer of the CBS News mainstay, in a memo to staffers Monday. “For nearly three decades, first at New York magazine and then at The New Yorker, she has reported on culture, gender, sexuality, health and the people and ideas shaping modern life in a way that is entirely unique.”
	

	Levy will join a growing roster of new faces at “60 Minutes.” In July, Bilton welcomed Ross Douthat, the conservative New York Times columnist, along with author Sebastian Junger, new CBS News correspondent Trevor Phillips and filmmaker Gianna Toboni to the show’s ranks. Longtime correspondents Leslie Stahl, Jon Wertheim and Bill Whitaker remain on the show, and have been joined by Norah O’Donnell.


	The whole assemblage replace a group of longtime correspondents who were ousted by Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News, in what she sees as a bid to make the program more interesting for modern viewers. Weiss believes the program is in dire need of a shake-up and has to be made more relevant to digital audiences and younger crowds. In late May, she replaced Tanya Simon, the show’s previous executive producer, along with correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega and executive editor Draggan Mihailovich. Scott Pelley left soon after following a clash with Bilton. Anderson Cooper chose to leave the program earlier in the year, ostensibly because he has been wary of the direction CBS News has taken under Weiss, an opinion journalist who has often worked to get more time for Trump administration officials and provocative voices and experts.
	

	Levy has been a staff writer at The New Yorker since 2008, exploring everything from the “Girls Gone Wild” series of sex tapes to the popular HBO series “Sex in the City.” She is the author of “Female Chauvinist Pigs,” an examination of why young women embrace raunch, as well as “The Rules Do Not Apply,” a memoir that analyzes her miscarriage, an affair, her spouse’s alcoholism, and her divorce.

	“Ariel adds to our truly exceptional group of correspondents and contributors for Season 59,” Bilton said. “They bring different journalism backgrounds, experiences, interests and ways of telling stories, but they share the qualities that matter here: curiosity, independence, incredible reporting, a willingness to hold power to account, and an instinct for the kind of stories people can’t stop watching.”

	The new group has been convened under pressure. The 59th season of “60 Minutes” is slated to debut September 13. In normal times, correspondents try to bank a piece before taking time off in July. Because of the abrupt overhaul of the program, however, there have been fewer staffers and producers to develop stories and segments.

	Bilton has other challenges. Morale at the program has been low. Previous management at Paramount turned the program into a bargaining chip with the Trump administration, which leveraged a $16 million settlement to end what has been viewed in many legal circles as a flimsy lawsuit tied to a pre-Election Day interview between Whitaker, and former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount made the deal as it sought to complete its sale to Skydance, the network’s current owner. Paramount’s capitulation spurred the exits of two senior CBS News executives — Bill Owens, the former “60 Minutes” executive producer, and Wendy McMahon, the former CEO of CBS’ news, stations and syndication businesses.

	Millions of dollars are at stake. The newsmagazine generated between $67 million and $69 million in advertising revenue in both 2024 and 2025 according to data from iSpot, and commanded the 11th-biggest haul of ad dollars of any show on CBS last year. “60 Minutes” is a dependable perch for one of the network’s top sponsor categories –- healthcare and pharmaceuticals — and counts drugs such as Rinvoq, Clairtin, Skyrizi and Vabysmo as among its biggest advertisers in 2026.

schema.headline: Ariel Levy, a New Yorker Staff Writer, Joins ’60 Minutes’ as Contributor

title: Peacock Launches Test of Membership Rewards Program With Perks Including NBCU and Bravo Merch Discounts, Free Pizzas
description: NBCUniversal‘s Peacock launched a limited new membership program in a beta test with a variety of perks — aimed at keeping them from flying the coop
body:
NBCUniversal‘s Peacock launched a limited new membership program in a beta test with a variety of perks — aimed at keeping them from flying the coop as streaming subscribers, as well as driving incremental revenue from marketing pacts.

	The test of Peacock’s membership program is available initially to a limited, “randomly selected” group of Peacock Premium and Premium Plus subscribers, according to NBCU. “Through a mix of NBCUniversal benefits, partner offers and exclusive experiences, the program will recognize and reward Peacock subscribers, deliver added value, and create deeper connections to the fandoms that power NBCUniversal,” the company said.
	

	NBCU’s test of the Peacock rewards program follows similar efforts by other streamers, including Disney+ Perks, which offers customers an array of different promotional offers and discounts.


	Launched in July 2020, the Peacock streaming service turned its first-ever quarterly profit for Q2 2026. Peacock paid subscribers totaled 48 million as of the end of June, with 2 million net additions during the period.

	As Peacock continues to test and evolve the program, NBCU said, additional rewards are expected to be added over time, including Universal Parks perks and experiences, NBCU content previews and early access to NBCU live events.

	On a recent episode of Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast, Matt Strauss, chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group, spoke about the Peacock membership program. “[W]e’re starting to evolve from thinking of this as streaming to entertainment, from subscription to membership,” he said. “Again, we’re always charting out what we see as the next white space. This is where we see, at least for NBCUniversal, the next wave of growth for streaming and the broader business as we’re continuing to build out where we see the big opportunity.”
	

	During the beta test, Peacock’s membership program will group participants in three tiers based on their tenure as subscribers: Gold (3 months-1 year), Platinum (1-3 years) and Diamond (3+ years), with select rewards tailored to each tier.

	At launch, members in the beta test will have access to the following rewards: 


An NBCU Shop 25% discount (for Shop at NBC Studios products)
A Bravo Shop discount (dependent on membership tier), with Gold members eligible for 15% off, Platinum members receiving 20% off and Diamond members receiving 25% off
A complimentary one-year Instacart+ membership (which auto-renews as a paid membership after 12 months); benefits include no grocery delivery fees on orders of at least $10, a subscription to New York Times Cooking at no additional cost (if activated by May 6, 2027) and free family sharing with up to three people
A Pizza Hut digital code that allows them to buy one menu-priced medium pizza and get a second medium pizza of equal or lesser value free (limited-time offer is unlocked after streaming three movies on Peacock)

schema.headline: Peacock Launches Test of Membership Rewards Program With Perks Including NBCU and Bravo Merch Discounts, Free Pizzas

title: ‘Spy Kids’ Actor Alexa PenaVega Shares Heartbreak After Deaths of Fellow Child Stars Hayden Panettiere, Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase: ‘Hug Your People Close Today’
description: Alexa PenaVega’s “heart is heavy” after the death of Hayden Panettiere, most notably because it marks the third passing of a fellow child star in 20
body:
Alexa PenaVega’s “heart is heavy” after the death of Hayden Panettiere, most notably because it marks the third passing of a fellow child star in 2026. The “Spy Kids” actor noted in a statement on social media that she rose to fame with and grew up alongside the likes of Panettiere, Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase. All three actors died in their 30s between February and August.

	“Hayden, Michelle, Daveigh… my heart is heavy today,” PenaVega wrote. “These aren’t just names from my childhood. They’re girls I grew up alongside, sharing a world that was exciting and also incredibly hard. We were kids navigating something so big, and not everyone had the foundation or support they deserved.”
	

	“Today, I’m grieving and holding their families close in my prayers and thinking of everyone still fighting battles we can’t see,” she added. “Hug your people close today.”

	PenaVega, Panettiere, Trachtenberg and Chase all came of age together in Hollywood in the 2000s. PenaVega’s breakout turn in 2001’s “Spy Kids” made her a regular at Hollywood premieres, where she was often photographed with her fellow child-turned-teen stars. Chase and PenaVega walked part of Disney’s “Freaky Friday” red carpet together in 2003 (one year after Chase voiced Lilo in the studio’s animated movie “Lilo & Stitch”), while PenaVega attended the premiere of Panettiere’s “Raising Helen” in 2004, among several other Hollywood encounters.

	Panettiere died on Sunday in Greenville, South Carolina, at the age of 36. Her death is currently under investigation, but there were “not any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances,” according to police. She was beloved for the television series “Heroes” and “Nasvhille,” but she broke out as a Disney child star in “A Bug’s Life” and “Remember the Titans,” among other hit roles. 
	

	Also beginning work as a child actor, Trachtenberg appeared in the ’90s Nickelodeon series “The Adventures of Pete & Pete” before starring in the family film “Harriet the Spy” in 1996 at the age of 10. As a teenager, she featured as Dawn Summers in “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” and later played Georgina Sparks on the teen drama “Gossip Girl.” Trachtenberg died in February at 39 years old due to natural causes, as a result of complications from diabetes mellitus.

	Chase, who voiced Lilo in “Lilo & Stitch” and starred in “The Ring,” died June 16 in Los Angeles at 35. The actor’s cause of death was AIDS, according to the coroner’s office. A secondary cause was listed as “chronic polysubstance use.” Chase’s father, John David Schwallier, told the New York Times that she had been homeless and had struggled with drugs since the age of 13.

schema.headline: ‘Spy Kids’ Actor Alexa PenaVega Shares Heartbreak After Deaths of Fellow Child Stars Hayden Panettiere, Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase: ‘Hug Your People Close Today’

title: Connie Britton Praises Hayden Panettiere’s ‘Brilliance’ After ‘Nashville’ Co-Star’s Death: ‘I Love You Girl. Sleep Easy Now’
description: Connie Britton has “no words” following the death of her “Nashville” co-star Hayden Panettiere at 36 years old. The duo starred together on five sea
body:
Connie Britton has “no words” following the death of her “Nashville” co-star Hayden Panettiere at 36 years old. The duo starred together on five seasons of the ABC country music drama from 2012 to 2016, with Panettiere headlining the series solo during its sixth and final season in 2018. Britton returned as a guest star during the final episodes. 

	“This was Hayden. Bursting with brilliance, shining so bright,” Britton posted on social media alongside a slideshow of photos of Panettiere and herself over the years. “I have no words for this sad song. Just heartbreak. I love you girl. Sleep easy now.”
	

	“Nashville,” created by “Thelma & Louise” Oscar winner Callie Khouri, premiered on ABC in October 2012  with Britton as Rayna Jaymes, a country music superstar, and Panettiere as Juliette Barnes, the rising country superstar who becomes Rayna’s rival. The actors earned critical acclaim for their performances. Britton picked up an Emmy nomination in 2013 for outstanding lead actress in a drama series, while Panettiere scored a Golden Globe nomination the following year for best supporting actress. Panettiere was also nominated for a Critics’ Choice TV Award in 2016.


	Panettiere died on Sunday in Greenville, South Carolina, at the age of 36. Her death is currently under investigation, but there were “not any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances,” according to police. The cause of Panettiere’s death has not yet been confirmed, but People reported that on the dispatch audio, which the outlet obtained, officials could be heard discussing an “overdose” and “cardiac arrest.” An official cause of death will be given following an autopsy.
	

	“Nashville” was Panettiere’s second hit television series following the breakout run of NBC’s “Heroes,” which starred in for four seasons.

            Our sources say there are still no leads in capturing Nancy's kidnappers or locating her remains.

            Nancy Mace is sending out thoughts and prayers to those social media users allergic to ink -- her ink specifically ... blasting everyone offended by her tattoos.

            Basically, Nancy thinks her tats are NBD ... but the internet ink haters are clearly up in arms!

title: Andrew Gillum Leaves Jail for Rehab After Alleged Positive Meth Test
description:
Ex-Florida Governor Nominee
                          Andrew Gillum Checks Into Rehab
body:
Ex-Florida Governor Nominee
                          Andrew Gillum Checks Into Rehab
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Andrew Gillum is swapping jail for rehab ... but the court will still be keeping close tabs on him.
      
    
            According to new legal documents obtained by TMZ, a judge ordered the former Florida gubernatorial candidate released from the Baldwin County Jail Friday ... so he could enter Cumberland Heights Treatment Center in Nashville.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Gillum must wear a GPS ankle monitor during his release ... and remain at the facility for at least 30 days, or however long it takes him to complete a drug and alcohol treatment program.
      

            The order says Gillum won't be allowed passes during intensive inpatient treatment. The judge says if he leaves without permission, he'll be considered an escapee and immediately arrested.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Gillum was taken back into custody earlier this month after prosecutors say he missed a random drug test and then tested positive for meth at a court appearance.
      
    
            His legal troubles began in July ... when Alabama cops said they pulled him over for driving erratically and found 3 grams of meth, 8 pre-rolled joints, cut straws, pipes and a bong.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Gillum is charged with felony meth possession and two misdemeanors.
      
    
            The order says if Gillum leaves the treatment center for any reason -- even after successfully completing inpatient treatment -- the judge must immediately be notified, and Gillum shall be returned to jail.

body:
Luigi Mangione
                          State Murder Trial Pushed Back ...
                          As His Lawyers Try to Get Case Tossed
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Luigi Mangione will not go on trial for murder next month ... the start of his state proceedings have been delayed after his federal guilty plea last week.
      
    
            A judge in Manhattan has given state prosecutors until October 9 to respond to Luigi's request to dismiss the case ... thus pushing back the previous September 8 start date.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Luigi's legal team filed to dismiss the state case right after he pled guilty to federal stalking charges -- arguing that the guilty plea now bars the state case from moving forward under the federal Constitution and New York's double jeopardy law.
      

            Hit team also accused state and federal prosecutors of using him as a "pawn" in a coordinated push to punish him twice for the killing.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Luigi is still awaiting sentencing in the federal case ... he did not come to a plea agreement with prosecutors, so he's essentially at the judge's mercy. Federal sentencing guidelines recommend between 24 and 30 years.
      
    
            Not only did Luigi plead guilty to stalking ... but he also admitted he killed Brian Thompson -- a bombshell statement state prosecutors could use against him if the murder trial does happen.

            The murder trial for alleged Tupac Shakur killer Duane "Keefe D" Davis is set to begin ... and we're live streaming the much-anticipated opening arguments.
      
    
            The trial's taking place in a Nevada courtroom nearly 30 years after Tupac was gunned down near the Las Vegas Strip.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Prosecutors say Keefe planned the murder and produced the gun used to kill Tupac -- though they say he's not the man who fired the fatal shot.
      
    
            He has pleaded not guilty to all charges against him.
      

            Keefe D regularly bragged about his alleged involvement with the murder in the years after the slaying ... and he was finally arrested by authorities in 2023. He's been locked up in the Clark County Detention Center ever since.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If convicted, Keefe faces life in prison ... which doesn't scare him because he's been in and out of jail for years. That said, we're also told he'd rather not spend his remaining days in prison.
      
    
            One source told us, "Prison is a dangerous place and horrible things happen there, especially when you're older." Keefe is 64.
      
    
            According to the Associated Press, the jury of 12 and 4 alternates was chosen from a pool of over 100 prospective jurors ... who were asked about their favorite books and movies, whether they had listened to Tupac's music, and whether they had strong feelings about gangs.
      
    
            Tupac was 25 when he was killed.
